articles.title: Things Must Be Busy At Milbank — See Also
articles.content:
**米尔班克律所提供提前入职，且“自愿”有真意：**
该律所向新入职律师提供提前三周开始工作的机会，并称因“客户需求异常强劲”而做出此决定。

**历史性团队律师跳槽：**
布朗·鲁德尼克律所刚刚从HSF克拉默律所的知识产权部门挖走了34名律师，创造了该所历史上最大规模的团队引进纪录。

**“你或许赢得了终身任命，但失去了终身信用”：**
本周，12名前联邦检察官向参议院发送了一封信，就特朗普的司法提名人选提出了他们的看法。

**苏珊·柯林斯反对托德·布兰奇的提名…自行揣测原因：**
她引用了滑行基金、司法部的政治针对以及其秘密承诺禁止邮寄药物流产等理由。几乎像她即将面临选举一样。

articles.title: Trump Warms To Ukraine Only Because It’s Winning; He Might Do The Right Thing For The Wrong Reason
articles.content:
俄罗斯与乌克兰的战争是二战以来欧洲规模最大的冲突，也是道德上最明确无误的战争。除非你被俄罗斯庞大的宣传机器所蒙蔽，否则绝对清楚俄罗斯无端入侵邻国，试图窃取一个主权国家，其战时策略是一系列日益严重的战争罪行，其领导人是一个残酷的独裁者，他认为谋杀是解决任何问题的最佳方法。在这场战争中，乌克兰是正义的一方，俄罗斯是邪恶的代表，这一点毋庸置疑。因此，MAGA（Make America Great Again）最初站在哪一方并不令人惊讶。

唐纳德·特朗普从未原谅乌克兰总统弗拉基米尔·泽连斯基，因为后者拒绝在2019年执行MAGA的计划，即迫使乌克兰调查乔·拜登的虚构指控，以换取共和党人释放国会已批准但被非法扣押的军事援助。换句话说，特朗普因泽连斯基拒绝被敲诈成为其犯罪的帮凶而长达数年的耿耿于怀。

MAGA对这场战争中正义一方的敌意在2025年白宫会议中达到了最令人尴尬的高潮，特朗普和JD·万斯在电视上无理地斥责泽连斯基。虽然这个真人秀时刻向愚蠢的MAGA支持者发出了诱人的信号，但更昂贵的是特朗普多次延误、撤销或冻结对乌克兰的援助，这不仅造成了生命损失，也损害了美国遏制好战俄罗斯的利益。

特朗普试图在每个方面破坏乌克兰的原因很多。俄罗斯帮助他赢得了总统大选。俄罗斯人口约为乌克兰的四倍（可能比乌克兰更腐败），这意味着更大的市场，适合特朗普帝国的阴暗交易。但最重要的是，我认为特朗普对弗拉基米尔·普京控制国家和在战争中毫不道歉的残暴行为深感敬佩。特朗普认为他是一个赢家。

然而，战争进行到四年半后，普京看起来更不像一个征服者。最初，许多分析师认为俄罗斯将在三天内轻松击败乌克兰的抵抗。就在今年初，乌克兰的形势仍然看起来非常严峻。现在，乌克兰正在收复比失去的更多领土，并深入俄罗斯打击普京的石油基础设施生命线。

普京无法阻止袭击本身，转而禁止俄罗斯人拍摄乌克兰无人机和导弹造成的破坏。一个赢家不会绝望地封口自己的失败。

最近，特朗普开始对乌克兰的事业表现出热情并非巧合。泽连斯基于7月28日出席了林赛·格雷厄姆的葬礼，在华盛顿期间，他与特朗普在白宫进行了关于“可能帮助”乌克兰对抗俄罗斯的“良好会谈”。

关键的是，特朗普在7月表示美国将允许乌克兰生产自己的爱国者导弹系统——一种强大的防御武器，美国军队在与伊朗的战争中已经短缺。特朗普在几周后部分收回了这一承诺，但并未完全否决向乌克兰转让爱国者技术的可能性，只要乌克兰继续看起来越来越像这场战争中的赢家，我愿意打赌交易将达成。

特朗普只尊重权力。他希望与他认为能让自己显得强大的人站在一起。他可能只邀请失败者进入自己的政府以便更好地控制他们，但在外国领导人方面，他喜欢赢家。

在这种情况下，如果特朗普想做正确的事出于错误的理由，我们不应该只是允许他：我们应该赞扬他。乌克兰需要所有能得到的帮助，美国为帮助乌克兰自卫投入的每一分钱都是对未来的明智投资。特朗普唯一实际能影响结束这场战争的方式是帮助乌克兰将俄罗斯逐出其边境。只要乌克兰继续获胜，他可能真的会这么做。

乔纳森·沃尔夫是一位民事诉讼律师和《零债务法学博士》（Your Debt-Free JD）的作者。他教授过法律写作，为各种出版物撰稿，并将财务和科学素养作为他的事业和乐趣。他表达的任何观点可能都是纯金，但仍然是他个人的观点，不应归属于他所隶属的任何组织。他也不想与任何人分享功劳。你可以通过jon_wolf@hotmail.com与他联系。

articles.summary:
The war between Russia and Ukraine is the largest European conflict since World War II. It is also the most morally unambiguous war since WWII. Unless you are a victim of Russia’s extensive propaganda machine, it is absolutely clear that Russia unjustifiably invaded its neighbor to try to steal a sovereign nation, that its wartime strategy amounts to stringing together a series of ever-more-heinous war crimes, and that its leader is a brutal dictator who thinks murder is the best solution to any problem.

When it comes to this war, Ukraine is good, Russia is evil, period. So, it’s probably no surprise which side MAGA originally landed on.

Donald Trump never forgave Volodymyr Zelenskyy for refusing to carry out the 2019 MAGA plot to force Ukraine to investigate Joe Biden for made-up nonsense in return for top Republicans releasing illegally withheld military aid that had already been Congressionally approved. In other words, Trump threw a years-long tantrum because Zelenskyy refused to be extorted into becoming an accessory to Trump’s crimes.

The most cringeworthy culmination of MAGA’s antipathy toward the righteous side in this war was the 2025 White House meeting in which Trump and JD Vance berated Zelenskyy in an unhinged (and televised) White House meet up. Though this reality TV moment served as a mouthwatering signal to the idiotic MAGA base, far more costly in lives, as well as in America’s interests in containing a belligerent Russia, have been the many times Trump has delayed, rescinded, or sequestered aid meant for Ukraine.

There are many reasons why Trump tried to undermine Ukraine at every turn. Russia helped him win the presidency. With roughly four times the population of Ukraine (and perhaps more than four times as much corruption), Russia represents a larger market for the kind of shady business deals the Trump empire thrives on. Most of all, though, I think Trump was simply in awe of Vladimir Putin’s grip on his country and his unapologetic brutality in the war. Trump saw him as a winner.

Four-and-a-half years into this war, however, Putin looks a lot less like a conqueror. At the outset, many analysts thought Russia would steamroll over Ukrainian resistance in three days. As recently as earlier this year, Ukraine’s situation still looked dire. Now, Ukraine is regaining more territory than it is losing, and striking deep inside Russia at Putin’s lifeblood oil infrastructure.

Putin, impotent to prevent the strikes themselves, has turned to prohibiting Russians from filming the devastation wrought by Ukrainian drones and missiles. A winner does not desperately seek to silence talk of his failures.

It’s no coincidence that Trump has been warming to Ukraine’s cause of late. Zelenskyy attended Lindsey Graham’s funeral on July 28, and while he was in town he and Trump had a “good meeting” at the White House about “ideas that could help” Ukraine in its war against Russia.

Critically, Trump said in July that the U.S. would permit Ukraine to produce its own Patriot missile systems — powerful defensive weapons that the American military has itself run short of in the course of its war against Iran. Trump somewhat walked back that promise a matter of weeks after he made it, but he hasn’t taken licensing of Patriot technology to Ukraine off the table, and as long as Ukraine continues to look more and more like the winning side in this war, my money is on the deal going through.

Trump respects only power. He wants to stand next to people who he thinks make him look strong. He might invite only losers into his own administration so that he can better control them, but when it comes to foreign leaders, he likes winners.

In this case, if Trump wants to do the right thing for the wrong reason, we should not only let him: we should applaud him. Ukraine needs all the help it can get, and every penny the U.S. puts into helping Ukraine defend itself is a wise investment for the future. The only way Trump can actually have any impact on ending this war is to help Ukraine eject Russia from its borders. As long as Ukraine keeps winning, he just might.

Jonathan Wolf is a civil litigator and author of Your Debt-Free JD (affiliate link). He has taught legal writing, written for a wide variety of publications, and made it both his business and his pleasure to be financially and scientifically literate. Any views he expresses are probably pure gold, but are nonetheless solely his own and should not be attributed to any organization with which he is affiliated. He wouldn’t want to share the credit anyway. He can be reached at jon_wolf@hotmail.com.

articles.title: AI Doesn’t Need Your Data. It Needs Your Workflow.
articles.content:
过去几年，人工智能领域的讨论大多围绕数据展开。组织担心员工可能将机密信息上传至公共AI工具，监管者辩论隐私、版权和数据所有权，安全团队努力建立守则规范AI系统中信息的进出。这些顾虑是真实的，且仍然很重要，但它们已经不再是最有趣的问题。

人工智能的下一阶段并非关于收集更多数据，而是关于理解工作如何真正进行。

全球领先的AI公司已使用大量公开信息训练了模型。但从书籍、网站或法律文件中无法学到的是，经验丰富的专业人士如何应对工作日中无数的小决定。AI不只是需要了解律师所知道的，还需理解律师的思考方式，何时会做出例外决定，以及在没有明确政策的情况下，为什么会选择某一方案而非另一方案。

这一转变有助于解释过去一年中许多观察者的困惑：为何OpenAI、Anthropic、微软、亚马逊和谷歌等公司大幅投资于企业软件、流程自动化和行业特定解决方案？这并非因为现有模型缺乏智能，而是因为仅有智能不够。AI代理可以独立地总结合同、起草邮件或回答法律问题。但将其置于真实的法务部门中，面对不断变化的优先级、例行的例外情况以及影响每项决定的数十年机构知识时，其局限性就立即显现出来。挑战不再是教会AI做什么，而是教会它工作如何实际进行。

考虑一下典型法务部门中工作是如何展开的。从理论上看，大多数流程都很简单。合同到达，经过审查、修改、批准、签署后存储。流程图让这一过程看起来井然有序且可预测。但现实远非如此。资深律师可能认识到某特定客户总需要不同的谈判策略。法律运营专业人士了解某业务单位可以绕过标准审批，因为已有既定的风险阈值。还有人记得半年前的对话改变了整个方法。这些决定都未在政策手册中记录，但它们每天都在发生。它们由经验、关系、情境和判断驱动，正是这些素质使机构运作，却难以在流程图中捕捉。

在UpLevel Ops，我们每天都面临这样的现实。作为法律运营咨询公司，我们常被邀请改进流程、实施技术或自动化工作流。但很少发现流程完全按照书面描述进行。相反，我们发现了多年积累的变通方案、非正式审批、未记录的例外情况，以及仅存在于资深员工头脑中的机构知识。清理这种复杂性通常是任何转型努力中最困难的部分。这也解释了为什么构建真正有效的AI代理远比简单地将大型语言模型连接到流程图更具挑战性。

在某种程度上，AI公司已达成与法律运营专业人士多年认识一致的结论：技术通常不是转型中最困难的部分。真正的挑战是理解机构如何实际运作。每个公司都有自己的文化、决策过程、风险容忍度、审批结构和未成文的规则。忽略这些现实的AI系统可能会产生技术上正确的答案，但往往会为该机构产生错误的结果。

从这个角度来看，近期大型AI公司的许多举措都变得合情合理。他们不再仅专注于构建更强大的语言模型，而是投资于企业平台、行业特定解决方案和能在机构日常工作背景下运作的AI代理。目标是观察决策如何制定，理解工作如何从一位员工流向另一位员工，并最终成为这一流程中更有效的参与者。帮助AI理解工作如何真正进行的机构，可能会塑造下一代智能系统。

每一个审批、修正、例外和判断都能帮助AI变得更有用，也使其变得更强大。对于法律专业人士来说，这意味着谈话不能仅止于保护机密信息。它还必须包括保护人类判断、机构知识和专业专长——这些一直是法律实践的定义。

这还有另一个重要理由。如果我们不主动，我们可能会设计出优化工作但忽视工作人员的AI系统。效率一直是值得追求的目标，但从未是工作的目的。人们从解决复杂问题、运用判断、培养他人、建立关系和贡献独特的人性中获得意义。这些素质不应成为自动化的意外牺牲品。

未来不应该是围绕AI构建组织，而应该是围绕人类构建AI。随着这些系统变得越来越强大，人类必须始终处于工作的中心。

Brandi Pack是UpLevel Ops的创新总监，拥有跨越法律、酒店、教育和技术行业的多元背景。在职业生涯中，她在惠普公司、康斯坦西酒业和Goodwill Industries等机构担任过各类战略业务运营角色，并在项目管理、培训、业务开发、法律运营和IT服务等领域有成功经验。她是工作场所人工智能这一新兴领域的思想领袖，特别是对法律领域的影响。
articles.summary:
For the past few years, much of the conversation around artificial intelligence has centered on data. Organizations have worried whether employees might upload confidential information into public AI tools. Regulators have debated privacy, copyright, and data ownership. Security teams have worked to establish guardrails around how information enters and leaves AI systems. Those concerns are real, and they remain important, but they are no longer the most interesting issues.

The next frontier of AI isn’t about collecting more data; it’s about understanding how work actually gets done.

The world’s leading AI companies have already trained their models on an extraordinary amount of publicly available information. What they cannot learn from books, websites, or legal documents is how experienced professionals navigate the countless small decisions that occur throughout a typical workday. They don’t just need to know what lawyers know. They need to understand how lawyers think, when they make exceptions, and why they choose one path over another when no policy provides a clear answer.

That shift helps explain a trend that has puzzled many observers over the past year. Why are companies like OpenAI, Anthropic, Microsoft, Amazon, and Google investing so heavily in enterprise software, workflow automation, and industry-specific solutions? It isn’t because today’s models lack intelligence. It’s because intelligence alone isn’t enough. An AI agent can summarize a contract, draft an email, or answer a legal question in isolation. But place that same agent inside a real legal department, where priorities change, exceptions are routine, and decades of institutional knowledge influence every decision, and the limitations quickly become apparent. The challenge is no longer teaching AI what to do. The challenge is teaching it how work actually happens.

Consider how work unfolds inside a typical legal department. On paper, most processes appear straightforward. A contract arrives, it is reviewed, revised, approved, signed, and stored. Workflow diagrams make the process look orderly and predictable. Reality is anything but. A seasoned attorney may recognize that a particular customer always requires a different negotiation strategy. A legal operations professional understands that a certain business unit can bypass a standard approval because of an established risk threshold. Someone else remembers a conversation from six months ago that changes the entire approach. None of these decisions are documented in a policy manual, yet they happen every day. They are driven by experience, relationships, context, and judgment, the very qualities that make organizations function but are nearly impossible to capture in a flowchart.

At UpLevel Ops, this is the reality we encounter every day. As a legal operations consulting firm, we are often brought in to improve processes, implement technology, or automate workflows. Rarely do we find a process that unfolds exactly as it appears on paper. Instead, we find years of workarounds, informal approvals, undocumented exceptions, and institutional knowledge that exists only in the minds of experienced employees. Cleaning up that complexity is often the hardest part of any transformation effort. It also explains why building truly effective AI agents is far more difficult than simply connecting a large language model to a workflow diagram.

In many ways, AI companies are arriving at the same conclusion that legal operations professionals have understood for years. Technology is rarely the hardest part of a transformation. The real challenge is understanding how an organization actually functions. Every company has its own culture, decision-making processes, risk tolerance, approval structures, and unwritten rules. An AI system that ignores those realities may produce technically correct answers, but it will often produce the wrong outcome for that organization.

Viewed through that lens, many of the recent moves by the largest AI companies make perfect sense. They are no longer focused solely on building more capable language models. They are investing in enterprise platforms, industry-specific solutions, and AI agents that can operate within the context of an organization’s daily work. The goal is to observe how decisions are made, understand how work flows from one person to another, and ultimately become a more effective participant in that process. The organizations that help teach AI how work really gets done may end up shaping the next generation of intelligent systems.

Every approval, correction, exception, and judgment helps AI become more useful. It also helps it become more capable. For legal professionals, that means the conversation can no longer end with protecting confidential information. It must also include protecting the human judgment, institutional knowledge, and professional expertise that have always defined the practice of law.

There is another reason why this matters.

If we are not intentional, we risk designing AI systems that optimize work while forgetting the people doing it. Efficiency has always been a worthy goal, but it has never been the purpose of work. People derive meaning from solving difficult problems, exercising judgment, mentoring others, building relationships, and contributing something uniquely human. Those qualities should not become accidental casualties of automation.

The future should not be about building organizations around AI. It should be about building AI around people. As these systems become increasingly capable, humans must remain at the center of the work.

Brandi Pack, Director of Innovation at UpLevel Ops, has a diverse background that spans the legal, hospitality, education, and technology industries. Over the course of her career, she has excelled in various strategic business operations roles at Hewlett Packard Company, Constellation Brands, and Goodwill Industries. Brandi has a successful track record in project management, training, business development, legal operations, and IT services. She is a thought leader in the emerging space of AI in the workplace, particularly as it impacts the legal landscape.

articles.title: Biglaw Is Now The Largest Employer Of New Law Grads
articles.content:
【今日金句】
NALP执行董事Nikia Gray表示："2025届法律毕业生中，超过500人的大型律所已成为最大的新晋雇主，吸纳了超过五分之一的毕业生。若加上251-500人的律所，约有四分之一的毕业生选择从事大律所工作。这一变化对法律教育和招聘行业产生了深远影响。"
NALP最新数据显示，2025届法律毕业生的就业率达到历史次高水平，大型律所正成为主导雇主，这与以往不同。

编辑Staci Zaretsky自2011年起担任《Above the Law》主编，欢迎读者通过电子邮件或社交媒体与她联系。

（来源：Above the Law《大律所成为法律新毕业生最大雇主》）
articles.summary:
Ed. note: Welcome to our daily feature, Quote of the Day.

Today, firms of more than 500 lawyers have firmly established themselves as the single largest employer of new law graduates, accounting for more than one in five employed graduates of the Class of 2025. When firms of between 251 and 500 lawyers are included, approximately one in every four employed graduates now begins practice in [Biglaw]. That transformation has profound implications for legal education and recruiting.

— Nikia Gray, executive director of the National Association for Law Placement (NALP), in comments given concerning selected findings on the Class of 2025’s employment outcomes. The employment rate for the Class of 2025 was the second highest in NALP’s history, with large law firms emerging as the dominant employer type, which is a major transition from years past.

Staci Zaretsky is the managing editor of Above the Law, where she’s worked since 2011. She’d love to hear from you, so please feel free to email her with any tips, questions, comments, or critiques. You can follow her on Bluesky, X/Twitter, and Threads, or connect with her on LinkedIn.
